title: History of Browserbase: The Browser for AI Agents, 2023 to 2026
summary: Browserbase history, 2023 to 2026: Paul Klein IV's memo, Stagehand, Director, $67.5M raised at a $300M valuation, and the move from stealth to agent identity.
body_markdown:
The first web browser ran on a black cube. In 1990, Tim Berners-Lee wrote **WorldWideWeb** on a NeXT cube at CERN, and the program called itself a **"HyperMedia Browser/Editor."** It could read the web and write to it. Thirty-four years later, a startup with a cube for a logo set out to rebuild the browser for a new kind of user: software.


That startup is **Browserbase** . It runs real web browsers in the cloud so AI agents can do what people do online: open a page, click the button, fill the form, log in, and bring the data back. In under three years it went from a solo founder's memo to **$67.5 million raised** , a **$300 million valuation** , an open-source framework with **more than 5 million monthly downloads** , and a seat at the table where Cloudflare decides which bots get through.


This is the complete history: the headless browsers that came before, the founder's one hard-won skill, every product and funding round, the fight over stealth and identity, and what the story teaches anyone building with AI agents. 🧭


> **TL;DR:** Browserbase, founded in January 2024 by Paul Klein IV, runs cloud browsers for AI agents and maintains Stagehand, an open-source framework with **5.78M npm downloads in August 2026** . It raised **$67.5M** , reached a **$300M valuation** in June 2025, and moved from stealth to signed agent identity.[Build agents that act on what they find →](https://www.taskade.com/agents)


## What Is Browserbase and How Much Is It Worth in 2026?


Browserbase is a San Francisco infrastructure company that runs web browsers in the cloud for AI agents. It was founded in **January 2024** by **Paul Klein IV** , raised a reported **$67.5 million** across four rounds, and was valued at **$300 million** after a **$40 million Series B** led by Notable Capital in June 2025. Its homepage claims **35 million+ browser sessions a month across 10,000 customers** .


The product is a simple promise with a hard problem underneath it. A developer asks for a browser, gets one in seconds, connects to it over the **Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)** , drives it with Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium, or Browserbase's own **Stagehand** , and disconnects when the job is done. Browserbase handles the fleet: containers, fonts, proxies, CAPTCHAs, regions, recordings, and a live view a human can take over.

## 🧬 The Prehistory: Browsers Were Built for People (1990 to 2023)


Every tool Browserbase builds on was made for a human at a screen or for a tester checking that a website still works. That mismatch, a browser designed for one person on a laptop and asked to serve thousands of machines on a server, is the opening Browserbase walked into.


*NCSA Mosaic (1993) made the web graphical and popular. Screenshot: Wikimedia Commons, CC0.*


The web started as a read-and-write medium. WorldWideWeb let Berners-Lee edit pages as easily as he read them. **Mosaic** (1993) and **Netscape** (1994) turned the browser into a reading machine for the public, and the write half faded into forms and content-management systems. The full human story lives in our[history of web browsers](https://www.taskade.com/blog/history-of-web-browsers-the-evolution-of-online-productivity) .


The machine story runs in parallel. It is the story of people who needed a browser without a person in front of it.


Year Milestone Why it matters to Browserbase


1990 WorldWideWeb, the first browser and editor, on a NeXT cube The web begins as read-write


2004 **Selenium** starts at ThoughtWorks as a JavaScript test runner Browser automation is born as QA


2004-2008 Beautiful Soup, then Scrapy Scraping without a JavaScript engine


2011 **PhantomJS** , a scriptable headless WebKit The first popular headless browser


2012 Chrome's remote debugging protocol over WebSocket The ancestor of the Chrome DevTools Protocol


2017 **Headless Chrome** (Chrome 59) and **Puppeteer** A real browser becomes scriptable on a server


2017 Browserless (hosted headless Chrome) and Luminati, later Bright Data The pre-AI hosted options


2018 WebDriver becomes a W3C Recommendation A standard remote-control API


2020 Microsoft launches **Playwright** , led by the former Puppeteer lead Cross-browser automation, and Stagehand's first engine


2023 Bright Data launches a Scraping Browser Hosted browsers sold to scrapers


The pattern matters. Selenium, Puppeteer, and Playwright were all designed so a test fails when a page changes. Developers bent them into robotic process automation anyway, and the scripts broke every time a website moved a button. The hosted options that existed before 2024 came from a proxy company controlled by a private-equity firm and a small bootstrapped service. Paul Klein's complaint about the market leader, as he told[Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/browserbase) , was blunt: *"they just jacked up their prices quite a bit and the dashboard hasn't changed in five years."*

## 👤 Who Founded Browserbase? Paul Klein IV and His One Trick


Paul Klein IV founded Browserbase alone, after spending years on one unglamorous problem: running web browsers on servers. He learned identity and login systems at Twilio, then ran headless-browser infrastructure as CTO of Stream Club, which Mux acquired in December 2021. He told his co-founders he would never start another company unless it was browser infrastructure.


### Twilio: the identity years (2016 to 2020)


Klein applied to about 500 internships and, by his own account, heard yes from Twilio and eventually Amazon. He joined Twilio as an intern in 2016, built part of its login page, and became tech lead of the login and identity-and-access team two years later. *"I didn't have a life. I just love my job,"* he told Latent Space. The identity background matters: it returns ten years later as his thesis about how agents should log in.


### Stream Club: the browser that ran on a server (2020 to 2021)


In the spring of 2020, Klein and his co-founders built **Stream Club** in a weekend: a live-streaming studio that ran in the browser. It raised a **$2.1 million pre-seed** and later added an API and SDK. To compose and edit video, the company ran web browsers on servers, and Klein became the person who kept them alive.


> *"The browser that you and I run on our local computers is not designed to be run at scale on servers… It's designed for a MacBook Air, not for a Lambda."* — Paul Klein IV,[Open Source Startup Podcast](https://ossstartuppodcast.substack.com/p/episode-184-building-the-browser)


**Mux** announced its acquisition of Stream Club on **December 22, 2021** , its first acquisition. Mux's press release framed the deal around browser-based live-streaming studios. Klein's own account is that Mux *"really wanted to buy our headless browser infrastructure."* He stayed at Mux, working on self-service and on browser infrastructure, until **January 5, 2024** .


### The vow


> *"I actually told my co-founders I would never start another company unless it was a browser infrastructure company."* — Paul Klein IV,[Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/browserbase) , February 2025


On the same show, swyx joked that Klein could become the Nikita Bier of headless browsers, a founder with one trick who keeps selling browser companies. Klein's answer: *"I truly do only have one trick."*


Year Paul Klein IV Lesson carried into Browserbase


2016 Twilio intern, then tech lead of login and identity Identity and auth, the future "agent auth" thesis


2020 Co-founds Stream Club, a browser-based streaming studio Browsers on servers are painful


2021 Mux acquires Stream Club (Dec 22) Headless-browser infrastructure has buyers


2021-2024 Works at Mux Developer experience at a great API company


2023 Publishes "An Internet Browser for AI" (Nov 30) The thesis, written down


2024 Leaves Mux (Jan 5), founds Browserbase alone One trick, done twice

## 📝 The Memo: "An Internet Browser for AI" (November 2023)


Paul Klein published **"An Internet Browser for AI"** on **November 30, 2023** , a roughly 3,000-word memo arguing that AI agents would need their own browsers and that nobody was building the infrastructure well. It came three weeks after Andrej Karpathy sketched an "LLM OS" with a browser among its peripherals, and it is still the company's founding document.


The memo's argument has two halves. First, large language models made web data easy to use: fetch a page, hand the HTML to a model, get a summary or a table back. Many modern sites only render after JavaScript runs, so that fetch needs a real browser. Second, and bigger, models can write the automation itself. Klein's clearest version came later:


> *"If you wanted to write a script to book a demo call on 100 websites, previously you had to write 100 scripts. Now you write one script that uses LLMs to generate that script for each website in real time."* — Paul Klein IV, Latent Space


On the Open Source Startup Podcast he reached for a database analogy. The bull case for Snowflake, he said, is that writing SQL used to be painful and now you can write as many queries as you want. *"When you decouple your human effort from the utilization of the infrastructure, the opportunity of the infrastructure platform goes up quite a bit."*


Klein compressed the whole thesis into one line on Latent Space: **"The future of software is software using software."** Your accounting app clicks a button, opens your email, finds the receipt, and uploads it. That future, he argued, needs new infrastructure, new interfaces, and human checkpoints, because AI is slower and less predictable than a function call. The browser is one piece of that stack, and the one he knew how to build.

## 🏗️ Year One: Infrastructure First (2024)


Browserbase spent 2024 building the hosted browser before anything else. It closed a $1.8 million pre-seed in March, joined AI Grant in April, raised a $6.5 million seed led by Kleiner Perkins in June, and a $21 million Series A co-led by Kleiner Perkins and CRV on October 29. Most first-year customers were switchers from homegrown browser fleets.


Most developer-tool companies ship a framework first and monetize infrastructure later. Browserbase did the opposite on purpose. Playwright and Puppeteer were already everywhere, and teams already had scripts. Klein's read was that the missing piece was a great place to run those scripts. *"The majority of our customers in the first year were switchers,"* he said, moving from DIY infrastructure or another vendor.

### Why a browser is hard to run on a server


Klein's favorite way to explain the business is to walk through what happens when you try to build it yourself. You write a Playwright script that works on your laptop, then you try to run it in production.


A browser session is stateful: it must stay open while a client talks to it, which makes it one of the hardest kinds of system to operate. The small traps pile up. A vision model looking for an emoji needs the emoji font installed. A headless browser has no screen, so you need recordings to know what happened. Chrome alone was too big for a typical serverless function, and a single virtual CPU made it crawl.


The first Browserbase ran on AWS ECS and Fargate, *"the largest Fargate customer in our region for a little while,"* Klein claims. The company then moved to Kubernetes with predictive scaling and warm pools across regions, and Klein has described Firecracker micro-VMs for fast, isolated startup. His rule for what to build in-house: *"I can't tell my customers, hey, we went down because so-and-so went down."*


```text
How a Browserbase session is wired (simplified)


your code / agent                 Browserbase cloud
─────────────────                 ─────────────────────────────────────
Stagehand, Playwright,   CDP      ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
Puppeteer, Selenium ─────────────▶│  session (one isolated Chromium)    │
▲                  websocket│   ├─ fonts, extensions, downloads   │
│                           │   ├─ proxies (routed per site)      │
│  live view iframe         │   ├─ CAPTCHA solving (optional)     │
└───────────────────────────│   ├─ identity / signed requests     │
human can take over      │   └─ recording → replay             │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
warm pools · regions · autoscale


```


### Proxies, CAPTCHAs, and the "sketchy vendor" problem


Browserbase owns no proxies. It routes traffic across audited providers and switches when one fails. Klein described the alternative, buying proxies and CAPTCHA solvers on your own, as feeling *"like you're buying drugs"* : pay in Bitcoin, trust the docs at your peril. Browserbase restricted some CAPTCHA solving to plans where it knows the customer, and it said from the start that it wanted to become *"an arbiter of good bots."* That goal becomes the Cloudflare story later in this history.


### Live view: a browser inside a browser


**Live view** is the feature that made Browserbase feel different. It embeds the remote browser in your own app as an iframe, streams page frames over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, and sends a person's clicks and keystrokes back. It exists for trust ( *"customers don't trust AI agents, at least the first pass"* ) and for human-in-the-loop moments: a CAPTCHA that fails, or a two-factor code sent to a phone.

## 🎭 Stagehand: Natural Language Meets the Browser (2024 to 2026)


Stagehand is Browserbase's open-source framework for controlling a browser with code plus natural language. Paul Klein and Jeremy Press started it in June 2024. It launched on October 29, 2024 with three methods (act, extract, observe), dropped its Playwright dependency in v3 (October 2025), moved into a browser extension in v4 (August 2026), and reached 5.78 million npm downloads in August 2026.


Stagehand started as a habit. Klein caught himself pasting a page's HTML into a model and asking it to write the Playwright code to click the right button. *"This really should be part of the frameworks themselves,"* he concluded. So instead of writing *"click the third red button that says Buy Now,"* a developer writes *"click the Buy Now button,"* and the framework asks a model to pick the right element.


### The three verbs


Method What it does Example instruction


**act** Takes one action on the page "click the checkout button"


**extract** Pulls structured data that matches a schema "the title, price, and rating of the top result"


**observe** Lists the actions available on the page "actions related to buying this item"


**agent** (added in v2) Runs a multi-step goal in a loop "search flights from SFO to Dubai for May 8 to 15"


The design choice that won developers over was restraint. Teams that already automated the web told Browserbase they did not trust AI to choose their steps, but they did trust it to repair a step that broke. So Stagehand kept the sequence of steps in code and added AI only where durability mattered.


> *"I really don't trust AI to do the steps I care about, but I do trust AI to self-heal or fix the step that went wrong."* — a customer view Klein describes on the Open Source Startup Podcast


### Why Stagehand is open source


Klein says it was never a debate. Every incumbent framework is open source. Automating every kind of website is bigger than any one team. And enterprise buyers relax when the part they integrate with is open: *"If you love Stagehand, don't worry, it's open source, you could go run this on your own infrastructure."* The hosted browser stays closed, because *"the value of Browserbase is that you have a team of 30 people constantly maintaining this infrastructure."*


### Stagehand versions


Version Date What changed


1.0 Oct 29, 2024 act, extract, observe on top of Playwright. Launched with the Series A.


(inflection) Jan 2025 Switch to the page's accessibility tree, better models, the Operator launch


2.0 Mar 31, 2025` agent()` for computer-use models, action caching


Python Jun 2025 Stagehand for Python and the hosted Stagehand API


3.0 Oct 29, 2025 Drops the Playwright dependency and talks to Chrome over CDP. Browserbase's benchmark: 44.11% faster on average across iframes and shadow-root interactions.


Multi-language Jan 2026 Go, Java, Ruby, Rust, and more (several alpha)


Server-side caching Feb 2026 Cached actions skip the model on a repeat run


4.0 Aug 10, 2026 Core logic moves into a browser extension. TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs at feature parity.` agent()` is removed, and` Stagehand.create({ browser })` replaces the old` env` setting.


### The growth curve


Stagehand did not take off at launch. Klein remembers *"a couple thousand weekly downloads"* in October 2024. The npm registry shows the climb that followed, and it shows no overnight success.


*Source: npm registry, package` @browserbasehq/stagehand` . Downloads include automated installs such as CI runs, so read the shape, not the absolute count.*


Two things stand out. The first jump arrived in **December 2024** (287,000 downloads, up from 13,000 in November), a month before the January 2025 inflection Klein describes. And the second wave in 2026 (2.2 million in February to 5.8 million in August) lines up with Browserbase's platform launches and Stagehand's expansion to more languages. On the Open Source Startup Podcast in September 2025, Klein cited about **18,000 GitHub stars and 400,000 weekly downloads** . The repository passed 25,000 stars in September 2026.


### Evals: the leaderboard next to the framework


Stagehand publishes a model leaderboard at[stagehand.dev/evals](https://www.stagehand.dev/evals) that ranks models on browser tasks by accuracy, cost, and speed. Klein's reason is practical. A model can top a coding benchmark and still fail at a date picker, *"the bane of the existence of LLMs,"* and a customer who picks the wrong model blames the framework. Publishing task-specific evals is how Browserbase keeps that blame where it belongs.

## 🎬 Director and the Vercel Playbook (2025)


Director is Browserbase's prompt-to-automation builder, launched with the $40 million Series B in June 2025. A user describes a task in plain English, Director runs an agent in a live browser, and the result is a reusable Stagehand script. Paul Klein calls Director an agent builder rather than an agent, and compares it to Vercel's v0 for websites.


Director began with an odd signal. In 2024, after Cursor took off, **dentists** started booking demo calls with Browserbase, three in two weeks. They were smart, owned their practices, lived with bad software, and had tried to wire Cursor and Stagehand together. They wanted *"something low-code."* The first attempt to launch Director, in early 2025, stalled. The team committed in late April and made Director the headline of the Series B.


> *"If you imagine v0 is for building a website, Director is for building automations to interact with any website."* — Paul Klein IV, Open Source Startup Podcast


On that podcast, Klein ran the first live demo in the show's history: Director verified a California real-estate license by opening the state lookup, typing the license ID, reading the result, and writing the Stagehand code as it went. Change the variable and the workflow runs again. *"Director isn't an agent, it's an agent builder,"* he said.


### The Vercel analogy


Klein describes the whole company in one comparison, which he spelled out on[Omar Waseem's podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=37bvJBmJ88g) in October 2025.


Layer Browserbase product Vercel equivalent What it does


Infrastructure **Browserbase** Vercel Runs browsers in the cloud


Framework **Stagehand** Next.js Open-source way to control them


Application **Director** v0 Generates the framework code from a prompt


The strategy is a vertical stack, not a horizontal spread. *"Every investment I make in Browserbase helps Stagehand and Director. Everything I make in Stagehand helps Director,"* Klein said. He warns that multi-product companies fail when they sell adjacent products to a different buyer too early. Browserbase sells one job, automate the web, through three entry points. Engineering is shaped like a pyramid: about three teams on the infrastructure, one on Stagehand, one on Director.


There is an echo here of Bill Atkinson's[HyperCard](https://www.taskade.com/blog/hypercard-history) , which let people who were not programmers build software by stacking cards. Director makes the same bet for web automation: the prompt that describes the task becomes the program that runs it.

One caution sits under every revenue number you will see for Browserbase. The company has published only "more than $3 million in revenue," and third-party ARR figures are estimates. Treat them as guesses.


On Latent Space in February 2025, Klein made a public, falsifiable bet: *"I can predict that Browserbase will be a billion dollar company one day. So let's check back in five years."* Four months later, the Series B priced it at $300 million.

## 🚀 How Browserbase Grew: The Product-Led Playbook


Browserbase grew almost entirely through inbound, self-serve sign-ups that expanded into large contracts. Paul Klein says most revenue is expansion revenue, that the company ran no retargeting ads, and that founder and team content, integrations with agent frameworks, and big single-day launches did the rest.


### Five growth levers


Lever What Browserbase did Klein's line


**Self-serve first** Developer and Startup plans, then contracts at committed spend Usage pricing ties revenue to customer success


**Integrations** LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and later MCP Be where agent builders already are


**People over logos** Launches from named employees, not only the company account "People follow people, not brands"


**A playful brand** Lego-like blocks and a cube, against dark-mode developer tools A reaction to "too much dark mode"


**Launch days** One big post per launch, all energy behind it "Nobody cares about your launch week"


Klein's LinkedIn discovery was humbling. Posts about his wife Julia go viral. Posts about Browserbase get about 100 likes. His conclusion was to tell your own story first and earn the right to talk about the product later.


He also named the cost of going first. *"I'm spending all this money teaching everybody about headless browsers. Then I have like two or three companies riding along beside it."* Director, in his framing, is market education, the way OpenAI's Operator made his mother understand what Browserbase does.

### The founder at 10 to 50 people


By late 2025, Klein described scaling from 10 to 50 people as *"miles harder"* than the three marathons and an Ironman he had finished. He took over engineering directly, with 25 direct reports ( *"I'm going Jensen mode"* ), and ran a Slack channel called **blocked by Paul** as a living to-do list. About 35% of the company were former founders. His advice to his earlier self fit in three words: **"Clarity drives output."**

## 🛡️ From Stealth to Identity: The Fight Over Who Gets to Browse (2025 to 2026)


Browserbase began by helping agents get past bot defenses with proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and a stealth mode. In August 2025 it joined the first cohort of Cloudflare's signed agents program, built on Web Bot Auth. By April 2026 it had reframed stealth as identity. The shift tracks the web's publishers, who started blocking AI traffic by default.


The turn was predicted early. In February 2025, Klein was open about the CAPTCHA business being temporary:


> *"We're building this company knowing that the CAPTCHA solving is short-lived until we figure out how to authenticate good bots."* — Paul Klein IV, Latent Space


By the Series B, Klein told[Upstarts](https://www.upstartsmedia.com/p/browserbase-raises-40m-and-launches-director) that Browserbase vets every at-scale customer's use case, a form of know-your-customer checks, and that it had *"never received a complaint or takedown request."* Seven weeks later, its traffic was at the center of a public dispute between Cloudflare and Perplexity.


He also named the structural reason a startup could do what a big lab would not: *"Imagine this New York Times headline: OpenAI CAPTCHA solving… Browserbase solves CAPTCHAs. No one cares."* His prediction for the long run was bigger than CAPTCHAs. *"Auth is the biggest thing that will prevent agents from accessing stuff,"* he said, and he sketched an OAuth-like flow in which an agent asks to log in as you, you approve on your phone, and the agent gets narrow scopes: book the apartment, but do not message anyone.

### How Web Bot Auth works


Web Bot Auth attaches a cryptographic signature to each request, using the HTTP Message Signatures standard (RFC 9421). A website or its CDN checks the signature against the platform's published key and decides whether to let the agent through.


### The axis of evil, and the armistice


Garry Tan's post landed the day the partnership launched: *"Cloudflare-Browserbase axis of evil was not in my bingo card for 2025 LEGALIZE AI AGENTS."* A browser company and the company that blocks browsers were working together. Klein did not take it personally. *"I don't think Garry meant it. He had a good hook,"* he told Omar Waseem, and he answered with a team photo. On the Open Source Startup Podcast he called it an armistice: *"me and Garry are all good."*


His defense rests on two points. Browserbase partners with many companies, not only Cloudflare: he named Okta, an investor, and Stytch, and 1Password and Fingerprint followed. And the program is optional. *"I describe it as TSA PreCheck for agents. If you want to get TSA PreCheck, you're going to get through security faster. But if you don't, you still have a way."*


He also makes a rights argument that anyone building agents will hear again: *"I should be able to have my agent access my software on my behalf… AI has a right to use your software just as much as you do."*


### The honest tension


One small episode shows why the old tools linger. When Google launched its Gemini 2.5 Computer Use model in October 2025, the public demo ran in an environment hosted by Browserbase. Simon Willison watched it appear to solve a Google CAPTCHA and wrote it up, then[retracted the post](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Oct/7/gemini-25-computer-use-captchas/) : *"it was Browserbase that solved the CAPTCHA even while Gemini was thinking about doing so itself."* Built-in CAPTCHA solving was still doing quiet work under a frontier-lab demo.


The identity story is real progress, and it is not finished. A Web Bot Auth signature proves a request came from Browserbase. It does not prove which Browserbase customer sent it, or why. Every customer shares one platform reputation, which is why a crawling dispute between Cloudflare and Perplexity could land on Browserbase at all. The missing piece is **delegation** : proof that an agent acts for a specific person with specific permissions. That is exactly the "agent auth" flow Klein described in early 2025, and it is why Okta, Stytch, and 1Password keep showing up in the partner list.

## 🔭 Eight Lessons From the History of Browserbase


The Browserbase story compresses into eight lessons for anyone building with AI agents: a founder's scar tissue became the product, infrastructure came before the framework, LLMs turned a testing niche into an automation market, and the company climbed the stack as the browser became a commodity.


1. **Your worst problem can be your best company.** Stream Club had to run browsers on servers, and that pain became Browserbase. The same lesson shows up in a Replit engineering post about[turning a headless browser into a video renderer](https://blog.replit.com/browsers-dont-want-to-be-cameras) : browsers do not want to be servers, or cameras.
2. **Sell the missing layer first.** Frameworks existed, so Browserbase sold the place to run them, then built its own framework, then the app on top.
3. **AI changes the unit economics of effort.** One script that writes scripts turns a fixed QA market into an open-ended automation market.
4. **Small verbs beat long prompts.** Stagehand kept act, extract, and observe, and fought feature creep. *"It's wrong to build frameworks with growth in mind… that's how you build slop,"* Klein said.
5. **Use the smallest sufficient primitive.** A browser, not a full operating system, covers most computer-use work at a fraction of the cost.
6. **The web's gatekeepers set the rules.** Browserbase's path from stealth to identity followed Cloudflare's default block, not the other way around.
7. **Trust needs a window.** Live view and human takeover made cloud browsers usable before anyone trusted agents to act alone.
8. **Commodities climb.** As hosted browsers multiplied, Browserbase moved toward identity, frameworks, and managed agents, the layers closer to the task.

## 🔮 What's Next for Browserbase?


Browserbase enters late 2026 with a clear lead in funding among pure hosted-browser startups, a framework that keeps growing, and a platform that now spans search, fetch, identity, and managed agents. The open questions are commoditization, delegation, and whether a company with this much agent traffic trains its own models.


**Commoditization.** More than ten funded startups now sell cloud browsers, and Cloudflare offers its own. Browserbase's answer so far is to own the layers above the browser: Stagehand, identity, and agents. The next two years will test whether developers pay a premium for that stack or treat browsers as interchangeable.


**Delegation.** Signed requests solved "which platform is this?" The harder question is "which person does this agent act for, and what may it do?" Okta's Cross App Access, 1Password's autofill, and Stytch's work point at the answer Klein described in 2025: scoped, approved, revocable agent access.


**Models.** Erika Bricky said in July 2026 that Browserbase is probably the largest aggregator of computer-use data generated by agents, and that Klein had tweeted *"we should just train our own model,"* while the company says publicly it is not doing so right now. If that changes, Browserbase stops being only a road and starts building cars.


**The bet.** Klein's own scoreboard is public. In February 2025 he predicted a billion-dollar company and said to check back in five years. The check-in date is 2030. 🔮

## 💬 Frequently Asked Questions About Browserbase


What is Browserbase?


Browserbase is a San Francisco company that runs real web browsers in the cloud for AI agents and automation code. Developers connect over the Chrome DevTools Protocol and click, type, read, and log in on websites the way a person would. It also maintains Stagehand, an open-source framework, and sells search, fetch, identity, and managed-agent products.


Who founded Browserbase and when?


Paul Klein IV founded Browserbase alone in January 2024, two months after publishing "An Internet Browser for AI" on November 30, 2023. He was an engineer at Twilio and then co-founder and CTO of Stream Club, a browser-based streaming studio that Mux acquired in December 2021.


How much money has Browserbase raised?


A reported $67.5 million: a $1.8 million pre-seed (March 2024), a $6.5 million seed led by Kleiner Perkins (June 2024), a $21 million Series A co-led by Kleiner Perkins and CRV (October 2024), and a $40 million Series B led by Notable Capital at a $300 million valuation (June 2025).


What is Stagehand?


Stagehand is Browserbase's MIT-licensed framework for controlling a browser with code and natural language. Its methods act, extract, and observe click, pull structured data, and list available actions. It launched in October 2024 and passed 5 million monthly npm downloads in August 2026.


Is Browserbase open source?


Stagehand is open source under the MIT license with more than 25,000 GitHub stars. The hosted browser infrastructure is closed source, and Paul Klein argues that its value is the team that keeps the fleet running, not the container files.


What is Browserbase Director?


Director turns a plain-English task into a reusable Stagehand script by running an agent in a live browser. It launched with the Series B in June 2025, and Paul Klein calls it an agent builder, the v0 of web automation.


How does Browserbase handle CAPTCHAs and bot detection?


It started with proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and stealth. Since August 2025 it has used Cloudflare's signed agents program and Web Bot Auth signatures, and in April 2026 it reframed stealth as identity with Verified browsers. CAPTCHA solving remains a separate feature.


What are the best Browserbase alternatives?


Kernel, Anchor Browser, Steel, Hyperbrowser, Browserless, Bright Data, and Cloudflare Browser Run offer cloud browsers. Browser Use and Skyvern pair frameworks with their own clouds, and Firecrawl and Apify specialize in crawling. Pick by whether you need a raw browser, an agent framework, or clean page data.


Do you have to pay for Browserbase to use Stagehand?


No. Stagehand is MIT-licensed and runs on a local browser, so you pay only your model provider. You pay Browserbase when you run Stagehand on its cloud browsers, which add live view, recordings, proxies, identity, and parallel sessions. There is a free plan, and paid plans start at $20 a month.


Where is Browserbase headquartered and how big is the team?


Browserbase is based in San Francisco. It had about 20 people in February 2025, 30 at the June 2025 Series B, and about 45 by September 2025, and a third-party estimate put it near 85 in August 2026.


Can Taskade AI agents browse the web?


Taskade agents search the web and read pages, and automations add Search Web, Scrape Webpage, and HTTP Request actions plus 100+ bidirectional integrations. Taskade does not click or log in on other websites. Teams pair a browser service for those steps, and Taskade provides the workspace where results are stored, reasoned over, and routed.
